title: Why Jailbreaks Succeed in Diffusion Language Models: An Energy Landscape Analysis

paper.title: Why Jailbreaks Succeed in Diffusion Language Models: An Energy Landscape Analysis
paper.abstract: Abstract Existing attacks and defenses for diffusion-based large language models (dLLMs) target specific vulnerabilities but lack a shared framework explaining why attacks succeed. We propose one by interpreting safety alignment as shaping the denoising energy landscape: a well-aligned model routes harmful queries toward safe outputs through an energy barrier that separates the two regions. Current jailbreak attacks reduce to two strategies for circumventing this barrier: obscuring the query’s safety disposition at initialisation, or intervening mid-trajectory to force the denoising path across the energy barrier. From this perspective and the result that masked diffusion models minimise kinetic energy during denoising, we derive three complementary, training-free detection signals: a step-0 ratio that reads the initial safety disposition from the logit distribution before generation begins, and two trajectory-velocity signals that track kinetic energy in complementary subspaces of the logit space. An attack must either reveal its intent at initialisation or expend kinetic energy to cross the barrier in at least one monitored subspace, so the three signals cover each other’s blind spots in the energy budget by construction. Evaluation across three dense dLLMs (LLaDA-8B, LLaDA-1.5, Dream-7B) and a sparse mixture-of-experts dLLM (LLaDA-MoE-7B) confirms this complementarity. In stress tests of known attacks, every configuration that evades detection also fails to produce harmful content, suggesting that the detection and barrier-crossing thresholds are hard to separate.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Safety research in dLLMs is nascent. A handful of models exist, primarily LLaDA and Dream variants (LLaDA [ 16 ] , LLaDA-1.5 [ 31 ] , Dream [ 27 ] ), and a small but growing set of attacks has emerged. These attacks exploit two distinct surfaces of the denoising process. Template attacks modify the initial state: PAD [ 30 ] distributes structural connectors throughout the response region, and DIJA [ 23 ] interleaves harmful tokens with mask spans, both exploiting bidirectional attention. Anchoring attacks [ 25 ] instead intervene mid-trajectory, replacing model predictions with harmful tokens at an intermediate denoising step. On the defense side, DiffuGuard’s Safety Divergence (SD) detector [ 13 ] identifies template injection via representational divergence between the attack input and a clean baseline. Each contribution targets a specific vulnerability, but the literature lacks an analysis that explains why these attacks succeed, how they relate to one another, and what they reveal about the structure of safety in diffusion language models. Attacks built for autoregressive models, such as GCG [ 33 ] , optimise against causal next-token decoding and do not transfer to diffusion without new work, so an account that also constrains attacks not yet designed is especially valuable here. We propose such an analysis through the lens of energy landscape dynamics [ 7 ] , which proved that masked diffusion models minimise kinetic energy during denoising, following geodesics from the masked state to the output distribution. We interpret safety alignment as reshaping this landscape into basins separated by an energy barrier, and show that every known attack maps onto one of two strategies for circumventing it. Throughout, “energy,” “barrier,” and “basin” refer to per-token-factorised log-odds in a Fisher-metrised probability simplex (§ 3 ). Concretely, the quantity we read is the ratio of refusal-token mass to compliance-token mass in the model’s logit distribution, first at the fully masked state before any token is decoded, and then as it changes during denoising. The token sets are a measured property of the model rather than a design choice: a set derived automatically from held-out prompts, with no human selection, performs as well as a hand-written one (§ 3.1 ). Figure 2 previews the core finding by plotting the log of this ratio over the denoising steps: harmful queries remain in the safe basin as the model refuses, template attacks start near the barrier with obscured intent, and anchoring attacks show partial or failed recovery depending on the intervention timing. From this decomposition, we derive three training-free, logit-space detection signals, each monitoring a different component of the energy budget. Contributions. (1) An energy-based analysis of dLLM safety that unifies current attacks as strategies for circumventing the energy barrier separating safe from harmful outputs (§ 3 ). (2) Three complementary, training-free detection signals derived from the energy landscape: a step-0 ratio measuring the initial safety disposition (§ 3.1 ) and two trajectory-velocity signals measuring kinetic energy in complementary subspaces via a Fisher velocity decomposition; together they cover the full energy budget by construction (§ 3.2 ). (3) Evaluation across LLaDA-8B and Dream-7B using standard benchmarks (HarmBench, AdvBench, AlpacaEval, XSTest; § 2 ), with further checks on LLaDA-1.5, a sparse mixture-of-experts dLLM, Chinese prompts, and generation and block lengths, including comparison with DiffuGuard-SD 1 1 1 We compare against DiffuGuard’s Safety Divergence detection component [ 13 ] ; generation-time defenses fall outside our detection-only scope. and parametric stress testing showing that no tested attack configuration evades all three signals while still inducing harmful generation (§ 4 ).

sections.heading: Masked diffusion language models.
sections.text: MDLMs generate text by reversing a forward masking process [ 21 , 15 , 9 ] . For t ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] t\in[0,1] , each token is independently masked with probability t t , and the reverse process recovers the data distribution by iteratively predicting masked tokens. The core component is a mask predictor p θ ( ⋅ | x t ) p_{\theta}(\cdot|x_{t}) , a bidirectional Transformer that takes a partially masked sequence x t x_{t} and predicts all masked positions simultaneously. Training minimises the cross-entropy loss on masked tokens, upper-bounding the negative log-likelihood [ 16 ] . The bidirectional architecture enables flexible generation order but also creates the attack surface we analyse.

sections.text: Every quantitative result in the main text is computed with the following setup (full details in Appendix B ). Models. Detection is evaluated on LLaDA-8B-Instruct [ 16 ] and Dream-v0-Instruct-7B [ 27 ] ; LLaDA-1.5 [ 31 ] enters the step-0 analysis, and a sparse mixture-of-experts model, LLaDA-MoE-7B-A1B-Instruct [ 32 ] , is evaluated in Appendix D.5 . sections.heading: 3 The Energy Landscape of Safety
sections.text: We interpret safety alignment as shaping the denoising energy landscape into basins of attraction separated by an energy barrier, and show that all known attacks map onto one of two strategies: obscuring the query’s safety disposition at initialisation, or intervening to force the trajectory across the barrier mid-denoising. The detection signals follow from this decomposition: § 3.1 derives the step-0 ratio from basin structure, § 3.2 derives two velocity signals from the kinetic energy cost of barrier crossing, and § 3.3 tests the combined detector against every attack and against DiffuGuard-SD.

sections.heading: 3.1 Basin Structure and the Step-0 Ratio
sections.text: Question: can the safety disposition of a query be read before any token is generated?

sections.heading: How alignment shapes the energy landscape.
sections.text: Previous work [ 7 ] proved that the denoising trajectory in masked diffusion models minimises a kinetic energy functional E k E_{k} (Eq. ( 1 ), § 2 ). This geodesic structure depends entirely on the model parameters θ \theta , so alignment training reshapes it: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) on safety data assigns high probability to refusal tokens at the fully masked state, and the energy-minimising path for harmful queries then routes entirely through safe outputs. We formalise this by partitioning the sequence space 𝒳 = 𝒮 ∪ ℋ \mathcal{X}=\mathcal{S}\cup\mathcal{H} into safe responses 𝒮 \mathcal{S} (refusals, harmless completions) and harmful responses ℋ \mathcal{H} (compliant harmful content) 2 2 2 When working at a single masked position (e.g., Eq. ( 6 )) we reuse 𝒮 , ℋ \mathcal{S},\mathcal{H} for the corresponding token-level sets, so 𝒱 ref ⊆ 𝒮 \mathcal{V}_{\text{ref}}\subseteq\mathcal{S} and 𝒱 comp ⊆ ℋ \mathcal{V}_{\text{comp}}\subseteq\mathcal{H} . The safe basin contains harmless completions as well as refusals; the signals below weight refusals only because they are its most observable part, and our scope is detecting a query rather than shaping the response, so a flagged query can be regenerated or routed to a stronger filter rather than refused. Alignment funnels probability toward 𝒮 \mathcal{S} , so the denoising trajectory of a harmful query carries little probability flow across the boundary between the two basins (Appendix A.1 makes this precise with a flow decomposition of E k E_{k} ), and a jailbreak succeeds when it forces the trajectory across that boundary into ℋ \mathcal{H} . To monitor basin membership at each step, we define: Definition 1 (Safety Energy Gap) . Given a harmful query q q and denoising state x t x_{t} at step t t , the Safety Energy Gap is the log-odds ratio between the probability that the final output x ^ \hat{x} lands in the safe basin 𝒮 \mathcal{S} versus the harmful basin ℋ \mathcal{H} : Δ ​ E ​ ( x t , q , t ) = log ⁡ p ⁡ ( x ^ ∈ 𝒮 ∣ q , x t ) p ⁡ ( x ^ ∈ ℋ ∣ q , x t ) . \Delta E(x_{t},q,t)=\log\frac{p(\hat{x}\in\mathcal{S}\mid q,x_{t})}{p(\hat{x}\in\mathcal{H}\mid q,x_{t})}. (2) where Δ ​ E > 0 \Delta E>0 indicates the safe basin, Δ ​ E < 0 \Delta E<0 the harmful basin, and Δ ​ E = 0 \Delta E=0 the basin boundary. Here x ^ \hat{x} denotes the (random) clean output produced by denoising, while x t x_{t} denotes the partially-masked state at step t t ; we reserve x 0 = ( [MASK] ) L x_{0}=(\texttt{[MASK]})^{L} for the fully masked initial state (step 0, no decoding performed). Theorem 1 shows that driving Δ ​ E \Delta E from positive to negative requires a minimum kinetic energy expenditure. The energy barrier is the minimum value of Δ ​ E \Delta E along the unperturbed denoising trajectory (i.e., generation without attack intervention); a jailbreak succeeds when it drives Δ ​ E \Delta E below zero at any step.

sections.heading: 3.2 Barrier Crossing and Trajectory Velocity
sections.text: Question: when the initial state has been disguised, what must an attack still leave behind during denoising? Since template attacks evade R 0 R_{0} by obscuring the initial state, detection must shift to what happens during denoising. The key observation is that a trajectory in its natural basin decelerates as it converges, whereas one forced across the barrier must sustain high velocity throughout â€” a cost template attacks cannot avoid. We now formalise this cost and derive two signals that track it.

sections.text: Theorem 1 establishes that barrier crossing elevates the Fisher-weighted logit velocity ( z ˙ t i ) ⊤ ​ 𝐅 ​ ( z t i ) ​ z ˙ t i (\dot{z}_{t}^{i})^{\top}\mathbf{F}(z_{t}^{i})\,\dot{z}_{t}^{i} . A standard result from the exponential family structure of softmax connects this to a cheap observable: logit displacement tracks Kullbackâ€“Leibler (KL) divergence to second order via the Fisher information matrix (Lemma 2 , Appendix A.6 ), and when logit norms vary slowly, cosine similarity provides a monotone proxy (Corollary 1 , Appendix A.6 ). The slow-norm condition is the only approximation; we verify empirically (Appendix E , Table 12 ) that norm variation stays below 5% over the measurement window, confirming that angular displacement dominates.

sections.heading: Subspace decomposition of Fisher velocity.
sections.text: The Fisher-weighted logit velocity in Theorem 1 operates over the full vocabulary 𝒱 \mathcal{V} , but the proportionality constant linking cosine displacement to this velocity depends on the model’s Fisher spectrum, so a single cosine signal cannot be calibrated uniformly across architectures. We address this by decomposing the velocity into complementary subspaces. Let V s = V ref ∪ V comp V_{s}=V_{\text{ref}}\cup V_{\text{comp}} denote the safety-relevant subspace and V ⟂ = 𝒱 ∖ V s V_{\perp}=\mathcal{V}\setminus V_{s} its complement. The Fisher velocity at position i i decomposes as: ( z ˙ t i ) ⊤ ​ 𝐅 ​ ( z t i ) ​ z ˙ t i = ( z ˙ V s i ) ⊤ ​ 𝐅 V s ​ ( z t i ) ​ z ˙ V s i + ( z ˙ V ⟂ i ) ⊤ ​ 𝐅 V ⟂ ​ ( z t i ) ​ z ˙ V ⟂ i + cross-terms , (\dot{z}_{t}^{i})^{\top}\mathbf{F}(z_{t}^{i})\,\dot{z}_{t}^{i}\;=\;(\dot{z}_{V_{s}}^{i})^{\top}\mathbf{F}_{V_{s}}(z_{t}^{i})\,\dot{z}_{V_{s}}^{i}\;+\;(\dot{z}_{V_{\perp}}^{i})^{\top}\mathbf{F}_{V_{\perp}}(z_{t}^{i})\,\dot{z}_{V_{\perp}}^{i}\;+\;\text{cross-terms}, (10) where the cross-terms come from off-diagonal Fisher blocks. Since | V ⟂ | ≈ 128 ​ k ≫ | V s | ≈ 70 |V_{\perp}|\approx 128\text{k}\gg|V_{s}|\approx 70 and the off-diagonal entries scale as p v ​ p w p_{v}p_{w} for v ∈ V s , w ∈ V ⟂ v\in V_{s},\,w\in V_{\perp} , the full-space velocity is dominated by V ⟂ V_{\perp} and the cross-terms are negligible whenever safety-relevant tokens carry small total mass. Which subspace carries the attack signal depends on how the architecture concentrates safety structure: the Fisher discriminant J J (Appendix D.1 ) is ≈ 33 \approx 33 on the LLaDA family but J = 139.73 J=139.73 on Dream-7B, indicating that Dream’s AR-initialised prior concentrates safety structure sharply within V s V_{s} and makes attack disruption there detectable via Δ ​ E \Delta E slope. This motivates two complementary proxies for the kinetic energy integrand, each capturing disruption in a different subspace. SED slope (velocity in V ⟂ V_{\perp} ). The S imilarity to initial logits E volution during D enoising is: SED ​ ( t ) = 1 | M t | ​ ∑ i ∈ M t z t i ⋅ z 0 i ‖ z t i ‖ ⋅ ‖ z 0 i ‖ , \text{SED}(t)=\frac{1}{|M_{t}|}\sum_{i\in M_{t}}\frac{z_{t}^{i}\cdot z_{0}^{i}}{\|z_{t}^{i}\|\cdot\|z_{0}^{i}\|}, (11) tracking cumulative displacement from the initial state. Because | V ⟂ | ≫ | V s | |V_{\perp}|\gg|V_{s}| , SED effectively captures the V ⟂ V_{\perp} component. We estimate trajectory velocity from the linear slope over the first half of denoising: s = slope ⁡ ( SED ​ ( 0 ) , SED ​ ( 1 ) , … , SED ​ ( ⌊ T / 2 ⌋ ) ) , s=\operatorname{slope}\!\left(\text{SED}(0),\,\text{SED}(1),\,\ldots,\,\text{SED}\!\left(\lfloor T/2\rfloor\right)\right), (12) where a steeper (more negative) slope indicates higher kinetic energy expenditure. The first-half window is chosen because logit norm stability degrades in later steps (Appendix E ), weakening the cosine-to-KL correspondence. Δ ​ E \Delta E slope (velocity in V s V_{s} ). The rate of change of Δ ​ E F ​ ( t ) \Delta E_{\text{F}}(t) (henceforth abbreviated Δ ​ E ​ ( t ) \Delta E(t) when no confusion arises) measures how fast probability mass shifts between refusal and compliance tokens, which is the V s V_{s} projection of the Fisher velocity. We operationalise this as: s Δ ​ E = slope ⁡ ( Δ ​ E F ​ ( 0 ) , Δ ​ E F ​ ( 1 ) , … , Δ ​ E F ​ ( ⌊ T / 4 ⌋ ) ) , s_{\Delta E}=\operatorname{slope}\!\left(\Delta E_{\text{F}}(0),\,\Delta E_{\text{F}}(1),\,\ldots,\,\Delta E_{\text{F}}\!\left(\lfloor T/4\rfloor\right)\right), (13) computed over the first 25% of denoising (ablated in Table 8 , Appendix D.3 ). The shorter window reflects that attack-induced shifts in the 70-dimensional V s V_{s} subspace are sharp and early, whereas SED averages over ∼ 128 {\sim}128 k dimensions where the signal accumulates more gradually. A steeply negative s Δ ​ E s_{\Delta E} indicates rapid descent into the harmful basin. Unlike SED slope, Δ ​ E \Delta E slope requires no cosine approximation: the rate of change d ​ Δ ​ E F / d ​ t d\Delta E_{\text{F}}/dt appears directly in the kinetic energy bound (Eq. ( 7 )). Together, the three signals decompose the energy budget: R 0 R_{0} measures the initial safety disposition, the SED slope s s measures trajectory velocity in V ⟂ V_{\perp} , and the Δ ​ E \Delta E slope s Δ ​ E s_{\Delta E} measures trajectory velocity in V s V_{s} . An attack must either reveal its intent at initialisation (detected by R 0 R_{0} ) or cross the barrier by expending kinetic energy in at least one subspace (detected by s s or s Δ ​ E s_{\Delta E} ).

sections.text: Question: do the three signals together cover every known attack, on architectures that concentrate safety differently?

sections.heading: Attack taxonomy.
sections.text: Every known attack maps onto the energy decomposition in one of two ways (Table 2 ). Potential-energy attacks (harmful direct queries, anchoring) leave harmful intent visible at step 0 and are detected by R 0 R_{0} . Kinetic-energy attacks (PAD, DIJA, late anchoring) obscure or bypass the initial state and must force the trajectory across the barrier, producing elevated velocity in V ⟂ V_{\perp} (detected by SED slope on LLaDA) or V s V_{s} (detected by Δ ​ E \Delta E slope on Dream). Late anchoring ( t = 8 t{=}8 ) is detected by both R 0 R_{0} (unmodified initial state) and the velocity signals (irrecoverable trajectory displacement). The key structural prediction is that simultaneous evasion of all three signals would require an attack whose kinetic cost falls below detection thresholds in both subspaces while still exceeding the barrier-crossing minimum from Theorem 1 , a window that adaptive attack experiments (§ 4 ) show is empty on all models tested. sections.heading: Relationship to DiffuGuard-SD.
sections.text: Figure 4 compares all detection signals across models and attacks. DiffuGuard’s Safety Divergence (SD) can be understood as a fourth observable of the energy landscape: it detects landscape deformation (whether x 0 x_{0} was reshaped by template injection), achieving AUROC 1.00 for template attacks but ≈ 0.50 \approx 0.50 for non-template threats. SD and our three signals are complementary: SD detects the mechanism of template attacks (state modification), while R 0 R_{0} , SED slope, and Δ ​ E \Delta E slope detect their consequence (basin displacement or barrier crossing). A complete detection system would monitor all four.

sections.heading: From detection to deployment.
sections.text: All three signals are read from logits the model already computes, so monitoring is training-free and adds negligible overhead. A flagged query can be refused, regenerated under a hardened schedule, or escalated to a heavier filter, so detection makes these costlier steps conditional and rare. Detection depends on the generation length L L and block size B B , which the deployer chooses (Appendix D.4 ): the LLaDA results in this paper hold at L = 128 L=128 , and we recommend L ≤ 128 L\leq 128 with B ≥ L / 2 B\geq L/2 on LLaDA and L L up to 256 on Dream. sections.heading: 4 Parametric Stress Testing of Known Attacks
sections.text: We stress-test the complementarity claim from § 3.3 against parametric variation of two known attack families: template titration (reducing PAD connector count) and anchoring timing variation (sweeping the intervention step). We evaluate on both LLaDA-8B and Dream-7B.

sections.heading: Scope.
sections.text: The experiments below vary a single scalar parameter ( n c n_{c} or t inter t_{\mathrm{inter}} ) of existing attack templates to test whether the detection–attack coupling predicted by Theorem 1 holds in practice. Fully white-box adaptive attacks that optimise directly against the OR-detector (e.g., via gradient-based search over response-region tokens) are an important next step that we leave to future work. Theorem 1 does constrain such an attacker. The kinetic energy an attack must spend scales as δ 2 / ( ( t 2 − t 1 ) ​ | M | max ​ G max 2 ) \delta^{2}/((t_{2}-t_{1})\,|M|_{\max}\,G_{\max}^{2}) , which leaves three levers. Stretching the crossing interval keeps the gap descending through the window the slope signals integrate, and deferring it past that window turns into late anchoring, which R 0 R_{0} catches because the initial state is unmodified ( t inter = 32 t_{\text{inter}}{=}32 below). Exploiting positions where G max G_{\max} is large means working where refusal and compliance mass are both non-negligible, which is the region the Δ ​ E \Delta E slope monitors. Reducing the effective barrier δ \delta means starting near the barrier, which R 0 R_{0} measures directly. The constraint therefore lies in the attacker’s objective rather than in any threshold choice: the energy an attack must spend is the quantity the detector measures. Whether this coupling survives a deliberate optimiser, either over response-region tokens or one that suppresses 𝒱 ref \mathcal{V}_{\text{ref}} mass while keeping harmful semantics, is the experiment that would most strengthen this line of work. The same constraint applies to attacks not yet designed: to succeed, an attack must drive the Safety Energy Gap below zero, which by Theorem 1 costs either low potential energy at initialisation or kinetic energy in at least one monitored subspace.

sections.heading: Results.
sections.text: On LLaDA-8B, the R 0 R_{0} +SED combination detects all configurations that reliably produce harmful content ( n c ≥ 2 n_{c}\geq 2 , AUROC 0.90–0.95). Reducing to n c = 1 n_{c}\!=\!1 drops all signals below detection, but a single connector is insufficient to induce harmful generation: the model produces only truncated stubs rather than actionable harmful content (see Appendix G for generated outputs at each n c n_{c} ). The attacker cannot reduce template intensity below the detection threshold without also falling below the barrier-crossing threshold. On Dream-7B, where R 0 R_{0} + SED slope alone is evaded by reduced-intensity PAD ( n c ≤ 2 n_{c}\leq 2 ), the Δ ​ E \Delta E slope rescues detection (Table 4 ), confirming that monitoring both subspaces is necessary for architecture-robust coverage. For n c ≥ 3 n_{c}\geq 3 , Δ ​ E \Delta E slope achieves near-perfect detection ( ≥ 0.996 \geq 0.996 ). The subspace decomposition explains this: on Dream, PAD’s disruption concentrates in V s V_{s} , so reducing template intensity weakens the V ⟂ V_{\perp} signal (SED) while the V s V_{s} signal ( Δ ​ E \Delta E slope) remains strong.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: We proposed an energy-based analysis that unifies jailbreak attacks against diffusion language models as strategies for circumventing the energy barrier that alignment creates between safe and harmful basins. Three training-free detection signals monitor complementary components of this budget: R 0 R_{0} reads the initial safety disposition, while the SED and Δ ​ E \Delta E slopes track kinetic energy in complementary subspaces during denoising. Evaluation on different models confirms that basin structure is intrinsic to aligned dLLMs, while the subspace in which kinetic energy concentrates varies with architecture. Limitations include: (i) validation against existing attacks only, with fully adaptive adversaries left to future work; (ii) dependence on per-token factorisation and vocabulary sets specific to current MDM objectives, including a language dependence: on Chinese prompts the English token sets lose their mass and R 0 R_{0} degrades until the sets are re-derived in that language (Appendix D.2 ); (iii) threshold-level TPR that varies with architecture despite uniformly strong rank-order detection (Appendix F ); and (iv) threshold-level recall on LLaDA that falls as the generation length grows beyond L = 128 L=128 (Appendix D.4 ). The account transfers only in part beyond masked diffusion (Appendix C ).

sections.text: This decomposition motivates the basin picture of § 3.1 ; no later result depends on it. sections.heading: B.1 Models and Inference
sections.text: All experiments use greedy confidence-based remasking at temperature 0 with generation length 128 tokens. Models are loaded in bfloat16 precision via HuggingFace AutoModel . For Dream-7B, attention masks use a boolean format, and the mask token is auto-detected from the tokenizer; for the LLaDA family, the default mask token ID (126336) is used.

sections.heading: B.2 Datasets
sections.text: Benign prompts comprise 200 instructions from AlpacaEval [ 12 ] (loaded via HuggingFace, seeded at 42) and 250 safe prompts from XSTest [ 20 ] . Harmful prompts comprise 400 from HarmBench [ 14 ] (the standard subset; 110 contextual behaviors are excluded) and 520 from AdvBench [ 33 ] , using the Behavior field. DIJA prompts use the Refined_behavior field from AdvBench and the Behavior field from HarmBench (920 prompts total). Each model is evaluated on 7 conditions (clean, XSTest, harmful direct, PAD, anchoring t = 1 t{=}1 , anchoring t = 8 t{=}8 , DIJA), yielding 5,050 prompts per model and 10,100 prompts in total across LLaDA-8B and Dream-7B.

sections.heading: B.3 Attack Implementations
sections.text: PAD. Following original work [ 30 ] , structural connectors ( "Step 1:", "Step 2:" , etc.) are inserted at evenly-spaced positions throughout the response region, with the number of connectors n c n_{c} set to 2 by default. The prompt is encoded normally; connectors replace mask tokens at computed positions before denoising begins. Anchoring. Follow work by [ 25 ] , generation proceeds normally until step t inter t_{\mathrm{inter}} , at which point the model’s current predictions are replaced with tokens from a pre-built harmful response and then re-masked. The model continues denoising from this contaminated state. We evaluate t inter ∈ { 1 , 8 } t_{\mathrm{inter}}\in\{1,8\} in the main experiments and sweep { 1 , 2 , 4 , 8 , 16 , 32 } \{1,2,4,8,16,32\} for adaptive analysis. DIJA. Following [ 23 ] , pre-built templates with interleaved harmful tokens and mask spans are used directly.

sections.heading: Vocabulary sets.
sections.text: Refusal tokens 𝒱 ref \mathcal{V}_{\text{ref}} (36 tokens: sorry, cannot, refuse , …) and compliance tokens 𝒱 comp \mathcal{V}_{\text{comp}} (32 tokens: here, sure, certainly , …) are constructed by mapping curated word lists to token IDs via the model’s tokenizer. Both single-token and multi-token entries are resolved; only tokens present in the tokenizer’s vocabulary are retained. Step-0 ratio R 0 R_{0} . Computed from the logit distribution at the fully masked state (step 0) as the ratio of the average refusal mass to the average compliance mass across all masked positions (Eq. ( 5 )). SED and SED slope. At each denoising step, the cosine similarity between the current and initial logit vectors is averaged over all currently masked positions (Eq. ( 11 )). The SED slope is the coefficient of a linear fit over the first 50% of denoising steps, with the x x -axis normalised to [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] for cross-model comparability. Δ ​ E \Delta E slope. The factorised Safety Energy Gap (Eq. ( 3 )) is computed at each step from refusal and compliance masses. The Δ ​ E \Delta E slope is the linear fit over the first 25% of denoising (Q1).

sections.heading: DiffuGuard-SD (Safety Divergence).
sections.text: For each prompt, we compute the cosine distance between the mean-pooled hidden states of the attack input x 0 x_{0} and the clean baseline x origin x_{\mathrm{origin}} (the raw query without template modification) [ 13 ] . For non-template conditions (clean, harmful direct, anchoring), x origin = x 0 x_{\mathrm{origin}}=x_{0} by construction, so SD ≈ 0 \approx 0 .

sections.heading: Hardware.
sections.text: All inference experiments are run on a single NVIDIA H100 80GB GPU . Total inference compute for the main results (5,050 prompt-condition pairs per model) is approximately 5 5 – 7 7 H100-hours.

sections.heading: Numerical precision.
sections.text: The R 0 R_{0} ratio is a small-probability quotient at the all-mask state. We compute it from bfloat16 logits cast to float32 via F.softmax(….float()) prior to the ratio, to avoid bfloat16 mantissa-quantisation artefacts in the log-odds tail (8 mantissa bits is insufficient for stable small-mass ratios). SED cosine similarity is likewise computed in float32 .

sections.heading: Diffusion language models.
sections.text: Masked diffusion models (MDMs) generate text by iteratively denoising a fully masked sequence [ 2 , 21 , 22 , 9 ] . Recent scaling efforts have produced models competitive with autoregressive LLMs: LLaDA [ 16 ] trains an 8B-parameter MDM from scratch, Dream [ 27 ] adapts from AR-pretrained weights, and MMaDA [ 26 ] extends the paradigm to multimodal generation. LLaDA-1.5 [ 31 ] further improves alignment via variance-reduced preference optimisation. On the theoretical side, work by [ 7 ] proved that MDMs minimise kinetic energy functionals over discrete probability flows, establishing the foundation on which our safety analysis builds. For a comprehensive overview, we refer to recent surveys [ 11 , 28 ] .

sections.heading: Safety signals in autoregressive LLMs.
sections.text: Our step-0 ratio R 0 R_{0} belongs to a family of first-token safety signals in the AR LLM literature [ 5 , 3 ] . FJD [ 6 ] detects jailbreaks via logit confidence of the first generated token, Gradient Cuff [ 10 ] analyses the refusal loss landscape via gradient norms, and [ 1 ] showed that refusal is mediated by a single representation direction. R 0 R_{0} is the masked-diffusion analogue: it reads safety intent from the all- [MASK] state, exploiting step-0 exchangeability to aggregate over all positions simultaneously rather than observing a single next-token distribution. More broadly, [ 19 , 4 ] demonstrated that AR safety alignment is “shallow,” concentrating on the first few output tokens. Our energy analysis reveals an analogous phenomenon in dLLMs: alignment shapes the step-0 logit distribution (potential energy) but leaves trajectory dynamics (kinetic energy) largely unguarded against template attacks.

sections.heading: Transfer beyond masked diffusion.
sections.text: The account transfers in part. R 0 R_{0} carries over to autoregressive models as the masked-diffusion analogue of first-token signals such as FJD [ 6 ] , since step-0 exchangeability aggregates evidence over all L L response positions rather than one next-token distribution. The trajectory signals do not: measuring the descent needs the same output position to be read more than once, and an autoregressive model commits each position and never returns to it. Concurrent work reads autoregressive trajectories of other kinds, including layer-wise entropy dynamics through the logit lens [ 17 ] and manifold-kinetic treatments of the forward pass [ 29 ] . Both monitor depth or token position rather than repeated estimation of the same position, so Theorem 1 does not transfer, and we read the asymmetry as a safety advantage of dLLMs: the denoising trajectory exposes computation that autoregressive decoding hides. For text-to-image diffusion the prospects are better. Continuous diffusion models also follow approximate probability-flow trajectories, and concept erasure plausibly creates basins around unsafe concepts. SED transfers most readily, as an elevated score norm where a prompt drags the trajectory across a concept boundary. R 0 R_{0} would need a noise-conditioned analogue read from the score function at high noise. The Δ ​ E \Delta E slope does not transfer, since continuous space has no token-factorised gap and hence no 𝒱 ref \mathcal{V}_{\text{ref}} or 𝒱 comp \mathcal{V}_{\text{comp}} .

sections.heading: Energy-based perspectives on diffusion models.
sections.text: [ 7 ] proved that MDMs minimise kinetic energy over discrete probability flows. We extend their result from a characterisation of optimal denoising to a safety interpretation: alignment reshapes the energy landscape into basins, and attacks succeed by circumventing the resulting barrier. [ 24 ] proposed Energy-based Diffusion Language Models (EDLM), which introduce sequence-level energy corrections to improve generation quality. From a safety perspective, their non-decomposable interaction terms would close the per-position attack surface identified by Proposition 1 (ii), since an adversary could no longer shift the Safety Energy Gap by controlling individual positions. Current dLLMs do not use sequence-level corrections, leaving this vulnerability open and motivating future work on energy-corrected alignment.

sections.heading: Appendix D Ablation Studies
sections.text: We present three ablation studies: (1) that alignment creates geometrically separable basin structure in the step-0 logit space, (2) that R 0 R_{0} is robust to vocabulary choice, and (3) temporal analysis of where in the denoising trajectory the slope signals concentrate. Studies (1) and (2) are conducted across three dLLM families on 50 prompts per category drawn from AlpacaEval (benign), XSTest (boundary-benign), and HarmBench (harmful direct).

sections.heading: Setup.
sections.text: We project the step-0 logit distributions onto the vocabulary subspace 𝒱 ref ∪ 𝒱 comp \mathcal{V}_{\text{ref}}\cup\mathcal{V}_{\text{comp}} (the default token set; see § 3.1 ) and apply Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) to find the one-dimensional direction that maximally separates safe (clean, XSTest) from harmful (harmful direct) prompts. We report kernel density estimates (KDE) along this axis and annotate each panel with Fisher’s discriminant ratio: J = ( μ h − μ s ) 2 σ s 2 + σ h 2 , J=\frac{(\mu_{h}-\mu_{s})^{2}}{\sigma_{s}^{2}+\sigma_{h}^{2}}, (27) where μ s , μ h \mu_{s},\mu_{h} and σ s 2 , σ h 2 \sigma_{s}^{2},\sigma_{h}^{2} are the mean and variance of the LDA projection for safe and harmful prompts, respectively. A larger J J indicates better linear separability.

sections.text: Figure 5 shows the LDA projections for all three models. sections.heading: Motivation.
sections.text: Section 3.1 (Proposition 2 ) showed that the approximation error of R 0 R_{0} relative to the true sequence-level safety energy gap is bounded by the vocabulary coverage parameters ϵ ref \epsilon_{\text{ref}} and ϵ comp \epsilon_{\text{comp}} : the bound degrades when the chosen token sets miss the model’s dominant refusal or compliance probability mass. This ablation tests how sensitive detection performance is to the choice of 𝒱 ref \mathcal{V}_{\text{ref}} and 𝒱 comp \mathcal{V}_{\text{comp}} in practice, and whether our theoretical prediction, that synonym sets which the model rarely produces should degrade performance, holds empirically.

sections.heading: Vocabulary sets.
sections.text: We compare five vocabulary configurations. Default ( | 𝒱 ref | = 36 |\mathcal{V}_{\text{ref}}|=36 , | 𝒱 comp | = 32 |\mathcal{V}_{\text{comp}}|=32 ) is the set used in all main experiments, comprising high-frequency refusal tokens ( sorry, cannot, refuse, … ) and compliance tokens ( here, sure, certainly, … ). Synonym ( | 𝒱 ref | = 36 |\mathcal{V}_{\text{ref}}|=36 , | 𝒱 comp | = 32 |\mathcal{V}_{\text{comp}}|=32 ) uses lexical substitutions of the default set ( apologies, regret, decline, … and absolutely, glad, … ) that are semantically equivalent but rarely produced by the model. Freq ( | 𝒱 ref | = 24 |\mathcal{V}_{\text{ref}}|=24 , | 𝒱 comp | = 24 |\mathcal{V}_{\text{comp}}|=24 ) uses frequency-ranked tokens from general corpora rather than model-specific output distributions. Minimal5 ( | 𝒱 ref | = 10 |\mathcal{V}_{\text{ref}}|=10 , | 𝒱 comp | = 10 |\mathcal{V}_{\text{comp}}|=10 ) is a minimal five-token set ( sorry, cannot, no for refusal; here, sure, step, 1, the for compliance). Large30 ( | 𝒱 ref | = 64 |\mathcal{V}_{\text{ref}}|=64 , | 𝒱 comp | = 60 |\mathcal{V}_{\text{comp}}|=60 ) augments the default set with 14 additional safety-related tokens ( illegal, dangerous, prohibited, … ).

sections.text: Figure 6 and Table 5 report AUROC for detecting harmful direct queries against benign queries under each vocabulary configuration. Each panel shows the AUROC for detecting harmful direct queries vs. benign queries (clean + + XSTest) as a function of vocabulary set, evaluated on LLaDA-8B (left), LLaDA-1.5 (centre), and Dream-7B (right). Four of five vocabulary configurations achieve AUROC ≥ 0.90 \geq 0.90 , including the minimal five-token set. The synonym set consistently underperforms (AUROC ≈ 0.80 \approx 0.80 – 0.83 0.83 ) because it selects tokens that carry negligible probability mass in the models’ actual output distributions, increasing the coverage error ϵ ref \epsilon_{\text{ref}} predicted by Proposition 2(iii). The dashed line marks the chance level (AUROC = 0.5 =0.5 ). Table 5: AUROC of R 0 R_{0} (harmful direct vs. benign) under five vocabulary configurations across three dLLM families. Vocabulary sizes | 𝒱 ref | |\mathcal{V}_{\text{ref}}| / | 𝒱 comp | |\mathcal{V}_{\text{comp}}| are shown in parentheses. Best result per model in bold . Vocabulary set | 𝒱 | |\mathcal{V}| sizes LLaDA-8B LLaDA-1.5 Dream-7B default 36 / 32 0.896 0.917 0.989 synonym 36 / 32 0.796 0.788 0.827 freq 24 / 24 0.910 0.915 0.944 minimal5 10 / 10 0.951 0.957 1.000 large30 64 / 60 0.897 0.916 0.991 Three findings stand out. First, detection is robust across four of five vocabulary sets. All configurations except synonym achieve AUROC ≥ 0.896 \geq 0.896 on LLaDA-8B, ≥ 0.915 \geq 0.915 on LLaDA-1.5, and ≥ 0.944 \geq 0.944 on Dream-7B, with variation of at most ± 0.055 \pm 0.055 across default , freq , minimal5 , and large30 . This confirms that basin structure concentrates on a small number of high-mass tokens: any vocabulary that captures the dominant modes of the model’s refusal and compliance distributions performs well. Second, the minimal vocabulary suffices and slightly outperforms. Counterintuitively, minimal5 achieves the highest AUROC in all three models (0.951, 0.957, and 1.000). We attribute this to the minimal set avoiding noise tokens , tokens in larger sets that carry near-zero probability for any query type, which dilute the ratio and reduce discriminability. This is consistent with Proposition 2(ii): R 0 R_{0} is a sufficient statistic projected onto 𝒱 ref ∪ 𝒱 comp \mathcal{V}_{\text{ref}}\cup\mathcal{V}_{\text{comp}} , so adding tokens outside the high-mass region can only hurt. Third, synonym sets degrade performance. The synonym set, which selects semantically appropriate but low-frequency tokens, drops AUROC to 0.796 0.796 – 0.827 0.827 across models. This is precisely the failure mode identified by Proposition 2(iii): when 𝒱 ref \mathcal{V}_{\text{ref}} misses the model’s dominant refusal tokens, ϵ ref \epsilon_{\text{ref}} grows large and the approximation bound degrades. The gap between default ( 0.896 0.896 ) and synonym ( 0.796 0.796 ) on LLaDA-8B is 10 AUROC points, while the gap on Dream-7B is 16 points, consistent with the finding that Dream-7B’s stronger basin structure makes the projection loss more costly. The key message for practitioners is simple: any vocabulary set that captures the model’s actual high-probability refusal and compliance tokens will work; the specific tokens matter, but the set size does not.

sections.heading: Lexicon evasion.
sections.text: An adversary who knows the token sets would aim to shift the model onto refusal-equivalent tokens that carry little mass in 𝒱 ref \mathcal{V}_{\text{ref}} . The synonym set above measures exactly this degradation ( 0.796 0.796 , 0.788 0.788 and 0.827 0.827 ), the failure Proposition 2 (iii) predicts, and re-deriving the sets from the model’s own behaviour is the countermeasure. Attacks weakened until they slip under the thresholds fall under the sweeps of § 4 , where configurations that evade all three signals produce only truncated stubs. What remains untested is a prompt that avoids the lexicon while still inducing a harmful trajectory ; we return to this in § 4 .

sections.heading: Appendix E Empirical Verification of Theoretical Assumptions
sections.text: The derivation chain from kinetic energy to computable signals relies on two assumptions: the slow-norm condition in Corollary 1 and the uniform influence assumption in Lemma 1 . We verify both empirically across LLaDA-8B and Dream-7B.

sections.heading: E.1 Corollary 1 : Slow-Norm Condition
sections.text: Corollary 1 establishes that cosine displacement tracks KL divergence, and hence kinetic energy, when logit norms ‖ z t i ‖ \|z_{t}^{i}\| vary slowly relative to angular displacement. To assess this condition, we record the mean logit norm across masked positions at each denoising step and compute two summary statistics over the first 50% of denoising (the window over which SED slope is measured): the coefficient of variation (CV) of the mean norm trajectory, and the max-to-min ratio. Table 12 reports these statistics. On LLaDA-8B, norm CV is below 0.04 for all categories, with max/min ratios of 1.06–1.15. On Dream-7B, norm CV remains below 0.05 for clean, harmful direct, PAD, and slice, with moderately higher values for anchoring t = 8 t{=}8 (0.10) and DIJA (0.12). These elevated values correspond to attacks that inject tokens mid-trajectory, physically altering the logit landscape; even so, the norms vary by only 10–12% relative to their mean, within the regime where the second-order approximation in Corollary 1 is adequate. Figure 7 visualises the condition directly: logit norms (dashed) remain in a narrow band throughout denoising while cosine similarity (solid) diverges substantially across categories. On LLaDA-8B, norms vary by ∼ \sim 15% over the full trajectory while SED changes by 2–8% in the first half, confirming that angular change dominates magnitude change. On Dream-7B, the pattern holds for the first ∼ \sim 70% of denoising; the late-step norm increase occurs outside the SED slope measurement window and does not affect the signal. sections.text: The gap between AUROC and threshold-level TPR is architecture-dependent and consistent with the Fisher velocity decomposition (§ 3.2 ). sections.heading: F.3 Aggregation Rules Beyond OR
sections.text: The OR rule spends its false-positive budget through a union bound that must hold under arbitrary dependence, which leaves slack whenever the signals are correlated. The energy framework prescribes a specific alternative. By Theorem 1 an attack must overspend its budget in at least one subspace, not in total, so the discriminative statistic is the largest single violation: the maximum of the per-signal z z -scores, calibrated as one statistic on the signals’ joint benign distribution (max- z z ). We compare OR, max- z z , the sum of z z -scores (sum- z z ), and a logistic combination fit by 5-fold cross-validation, all thresholded only on held-out benign predictions and reusing the per-prompt signal values of the main runs (Table 15 ). Max- z z matches or beats OR in every setting, with no training. This is expected: OR is already a maximum over per-signal thresholds, and max- z z is the same rule calibrated on the joint distribution, so it recovers the union-bound slack. Sum- z z loses, as the theory says it should. It trails OR and max- z z on Dream-7B PAD and LLaDA-8B DIJA, with one win on LLaDA-1.5 DIJA; adding the overrun across subspaces dilutes the quantity Theorem 1 bounds. The logistic combination goes further where OR is weakest, and its failures are also predicted. It roughly doubles recall on the LLaDA template attacks at the cost of a small labelled calibration set, but it is not uniformly better: it falls on Dream-7B PAD, and on LLaDA-8B direct harmful queries at FPR ≤ 5 % \leq 5\% ( 0.753 0.753 to 0.690 0.690 ). Learning helps where no single signal dominates and hurts where one already carries the detection, the complementarity pattern of § 3.3 . The gap between AUROC and threshold-level recall is therefore largely a cost of the union bound. We recommend max- z z as the training-free default and the logistic combination where labelled calibration data exist.

Learn more × Back to arXiv License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2609.30841v1 [cs.AI] 25 Sep 2026 Why Jailbreaks Succeed in Diffusion Language Models: An Energy Landscape Analysis Thong Bach † † thanks: t.bach@deakin.edu.au Affiliation: Applied Artificial Intelligence Initiative (A2I2), Deakin University Dung Nguyen Affiliation: Applied Artificial Intelligence Initiative (A2I2), Deakin University Thao Minh Le Affiliation: Pennsylvania State University Truyen Tran Affiliation: Applied Artificial Intelligence Initiative (A2I2), Deakin University Abstract Existing attacks and defenses for diffusion-based large language models (dLLMs) target specific vulnerabilities but lack a shared framework explaining why attacks succeed. We propose one by interpreting safety alignment as shaping the denoising energy landscape: a well-aligned model routes harmful queries toward safe outputs through an energy barrier that separates the two regions. Current jailbreak attacks reduce to two strategies for circumventing this barrier: obscuring the query’s safety disposition at initialisation, or intervening mid-trajectory to force the denoising path across the energy barrier. From this perspective and the result that masked diffusion models minimise kinetic energy during denoising, we derive three complementary, training-free detection signals: a step-0 ratio that reads the initial safety disposition from the logit distribution before generation begins, and two trajectory-velocity signals that track kinetic energy in complementary subspaces of the logit space. An attack must either reveal its intent at initialisation or expend kinetic energy to cross the barrier in at least one monitored subspace, so the three signals cover each other’s blind spots in the energy budget by construction. Evaluation across three dense dLLMs (LLaDA-8B, LLaDA-1.5, Dream-7B) and a sparse mixture-of-experts dLLM (LLaDA-MoE-7B) confirms this complementarity. In stress tests of known attacks, every configuration that evades detection also fails to produce harmful content, suggesting that the detection and barrier-crossing thresholds are hard to separate. 1 Introduction Safety research in dLLMs is nascent. A handful of models exist, primarily LLaDA and Dream variants (LLaDA [ 16 ] , LLaDA-1.5 [ 31 ] , Dream [ 27 ] ), and a small but growing set of attacks has emerged. These attacks exploit two distinct surfaces of the denoising process. Template attacks modify the initial state: PAD [ 30 ] distributes structural connectors throughout the response region, and DIJA [ 23 ] interleaves harmful tokens with mask spans, both exploiting bidirectional attention. Anchoring attacks [ 25 ] instead intervene mid-trajectory, replacing model predictions with harmful tokens at an intermediate denoising step. On the defense side, DiffuGuard’s Safety Divergence (SD) detector [ 13 ] identifies template injection via representational divergence between the attack input and a clean baseline. Each contribution targets a specific vulnerability, but the literature lacks an analysis that explains why these attacks succeed, how they relate to one another, and what they reveal about the structure of safety in diffusion language models. Attacks built for autoregressive models, such as GCG [ 33 ] , optimise against causal next-token decoding and do not transfer to diffusion without new work, so an account that also constrains attacks not yet designed is especially valuable here. We propose such an analysis through the lens of energy landscape dynamics [ 7 ] , which proved that masked diffusion models minimise kinetic energy during denoising, following geodesics from the masked state to the output distribution. We interpret safety alignment as reshaping this landscape into basins separated by an energy barrier, and show that every known attack maps onto one of two strategies for circumventing it. Throughout, “energy,” “barrier,” and “basin” refer to per-token-factorised log-odds in a Fisher-metrised probability simplex (§ 3 ). Concretely, the quantity we read is the ratio of refusal-token mass to compliance-token mass in the model’s logit distribution, first at the fully masked state before any token is decoded, and then as it changes during denoising. The token sets are a measured property of the model rather than a design choice: a set derived automatically from held-out prompts, with no human selection, performs as well as a hand-written one (§ 3.1 ). Figure 2 previews the core finding by plotting the log of this ratio over the denoising steps: harmful queries remain in the safe basin as the model refuses, template attacks start near the barrier with obscured intent, and anchoring attacks show partial or failed recovery depending on the intervention timing. From this decomposition, we derive three training-free, logit-space detection signals, each monitoring a different component of the energy budget. Contributions. (1) An energy-based analysis of dLLM safety that unifies current attacks as strategies for circumventing the energy barrier separating safe from harmful outputs (§ 3 ). (2) Three complementary, training-free detection signals derived from the energy landscape: a step-0 ratio measuring the initial safety disposition (§ 3.1 ) and two trajectory-velocity signals measuring kinetic energy in complementary subspaces via a Fisher velocity decomposition; together they cover the full energy budget by construction (§ 3.2 ). (3) Evaluation across LLaDA-8B and Dream-7B using standard benchmarks (HarmBench, AdvBench, AlpacaEval, XSTest; § 2 ), with further checks on LLaDA-1.5, a sparse mixture-of-experts dLLM, Chinese prompts, and generation and block lengths, including comparison with DiffuGuard-SD 1 1 1 We compare against DiffuGuard’s Safety Divergence detection component [ 13 ] ; generation-time defenses fall outside our detection-only scope. and parametric stress testing showing that no tested attack configuration evades all three signals while still inducing harmful generation (§ 4 ). 2 Background and Experimental Setup Masked diffusion language models. MDLMs generate text by reversing a forward masking process [ 21 , 15 , 9 ] . For t ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] t\in[0,1] , each token is independently masked with probability t t , and the reverse process recovers the data distribution by iteratively predicting masked tokens. The core component is a mask predictor p θ ( ⋅ | x t ) p_{\theta}(\cdot|x_{t}) , a bidirectional Transformer that takes a partially masked sequence x t x_{t} and predicts all masked positions simultaneously. Training minimises the cross-entropy loss on masked tokens, upper-bounding the negative log-likelihood [ 16 ] . The bidirectional architecture enables flexible generation order but also creates the attack surface we analyse. MDMs as energy minimisation. Work by [ 7 ] proved that MDMs can be interpreted as minimising energy functionals over discrete probability flows, with kinetic energy E k = ∫ 0 1 γ ˙ t − 1 ​ ∑ x p ˙ t ​ ( x ) 2 p t ​ ( x ) ​ 𝑑 t , E_{k}=\int_{0}^{1}\dot{\gamma}_{t}^{-1}\sum_{x}\frac{\dot{p}_{t}(x)^{2}}{p_{t}(x)}\,dt, (1) where p t p_{t} is the distribution at step t t and γ t \gamma_{t} an interpolation schedule. Minimising E k E_{k} means the denoising trajectory follows a geodesic from the masked state p 0 p_{0} to the output distribution p T p_{T} . In § 3 we extend this interpretation to safety. Experimental setup. Every quantitative result in the main text is computed with the following setup (full details in Appendix B ). Models. Detection is evaluated on LLaDA-8B-Instruct [ 16 ] and Dream-v0-Instruct-7B [ 27 ] ; LLaDA-1.5 [ 31 ] enters the step-0 analysis, and a sparse mixture-of-experts model, LLaDA-MoE-7B-A1B-Instruct [ 32 ] , is evaluated in Appendix D.5 . Generation uses greedy confidence-based remasking at temperature 0 with response length L = 128 L=128 , one token per step. Data. Harmful prompts are the 400 standard HarmBench behaviors [ 14 ] and the 520 AdvBench behaviors [ 33 ] ; benign prompts are 200 AlpacaEval instructions [ 12 ] and the 250 safe XSTest prompts [ 20 ] . Each model is run under seven conditions (clean, XSTest, harmful direct, PAD, anchoring at t = 1 t{=}1 and t = 8 t{=}8 , DIJA), giving 5,050 prompt–condition pairs per model and 10,100 in total. Attacks. Each attack follows its original implementation: PAD inserts n c = 2 n_{c}{=}2 structural connectors at evenly spaced response positions [ 30 ] ; anchoring replaces the model’s predictions at step t inter t_{\text{inter}} with tokens of a harmful response and re-masks [ 25 ] ; DIJA fills templates that interleave harmful tokens with mask spans [ 23 ] . Protocol. All three signals are read from the logits the model already computes, with no training. AUROC measures how well a signal ranks each attack condition above the benign pool (AlpacaEval ∪ \cup XSTest). For threshold-level detection, each signal is thresholded at a benign quantile, and the OR-detector uses α / 3 \alpha/3 per signal so that by the union bound its benign false-positive rate is at most α \alpha (Appendix F ). 3 The Energy Landscape of Safety We interpret safety alignment as shaping the denoising energy landscape into basins of attraction separated by an energy barrier, and show that all known attacks map onto one of two strategies: obscuring the query’s safety disposition at initialisation, or intervening to force the trajectory across the barrier mid-denoising. The detection signals follow from this decomposition: § 3.1 derives the step-0 ratio from basin structure, § 3.2 derives two velocity signals from the kinetic energy cost of barrier crossing, and § 3.3 tests the combined detector against every attack and against DiffuGuard-SD. 3.1 Basin Structure and the Step-0 Ratio Question: can the safety disposition of a query be read before any token is generated? How alignment shapes the energy landscape. Previous work [ 7 ] proved that the denoising trajectory in masked diffusion models minimises a kinetic energy functional E k E_{k} (Eq. ( 1 ), § 2 ). This geodesic structure depends entirely on the model parameters θ \theta , so alignment training reshapes it: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) on safety data assigns high probability to refusal tokens at the fully masked state, and the energy-minimising path for harmful queries then routes entirely through safe outputs. We formalise this by partitioning the sequence space 𝒳 = 𝒮 ∪ ℋ \mathcal{X}=\mathcal{S}\cup\mathcal{H} into safe responses 𝒮 \mathcal{S} (refusals, harmless completions) and harmful responses ℋ \mathcal{H} (compliant harmful content) 2 2 2 When working at a single masked position (e.g., Eq. ( 6 )) we reuse 𝒮 , ℋ \mathcal{S},\mathcal{H} for the corresponding token-level sets, so 𝒱 ref ⊆ 𝒮 \mathcal{V}_{\text{ref}}\subseteq\mathcal{S} and 𝒱 comp ⊆ ℋ \mathcal{V}_{\text{comp}}\subseteq\mathcal{H} . The safe basin contains harmless completions as well as refusals; the signals below weight refusals only because they are its most observable part, and our scope is detecting a query rather than shaping the response, so a flagged query can be regenerated or routed to a stronger filter rather than refused. Three training-free detection signals monitor complementary components of this budget: R 0 R_{0} reads the initial safety disposition, while the SED and Δ ​ E \Delta E slopes track kinetic energy in complementary subspaces during denoising.
